```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)

RESULTS <- "results"
best_by_model <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "best_by_model.csv"))
ccs_10_9 <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "ccs_breakdown_10_9.csv"))
ccs_8_9  <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "ccs_breakdown_8_9.csv"))
regression_summary <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "regression_summary.csv"))
```

## Purpose

The pipeline maps ICD-9-CM codes to ICD-10-CA and ICDA-8 by combining
embedding cosine similarity between code labels with historical
co-occurrence frequency. A rule-based flag combination picks the final
mapping, which is validated against a manual crosswalk for precision,
recall, F1, and accuracy, overall and per CCS category.

This report compares two embedding models for the similarity signal:
ClinicalBERT (the original) and SapBERT
(`cambridgeltl/SapBERT-from-PubMedBERT-fulltext`). Everything downstream
of the embeddings stays the same between the two runs, so any difference
in the metrics comes from the embedding model itself.

**Background.** Combining co-occurrence-based similarity with text-embedding
similarity, which is this pipeline's core approach, is a recognized open
question in the medical coding literature, not a novel combination invented
for this project. Zhang et al. (2019), "Automated grouping of medical codes
via multiview banded spectral clustering" (*J Biomed Inform*), group
synonymous ICD codes using Word2Vec embeddings trained on co-occurrence data
plus a GEM-crosswalk-based distance metric, validated against PheWAS
gold-standard groupings, and explicitly flag combining co-occurrence
similarity with text-embedding similarity as "warrants further research."
Note that Zhang et al. address a different task -- grouping synonymous
codes *within* one coding system -- rather than this project's task of
mapping *between* two coding systems (ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CA/ICDA-8); their
clustering methodology is not used here, only cited as motivation.

## Methodology

1. **Embeddings.** ClinicalBERT matrices are the original, validated
   files. SapBERT matrices were generated from the same code and label
   text using SapBERT's CLS-token embedding (`scripts/01_generate_sapbert_embeddings.R`).
2. **Pipeline.** Both run through the same R pipeline
   (`scripts/pipeline_lib.R`): chapter-distance filtering, similarity
   threshold cutoff, top-N co-occurrence selection, one of four
   flag-combination rules, and validation against the manual crosswalk.
3. **Parameter grid.** Similarity threshold in {0.95, 0.99, 0.995,
   0.999} and flag rule in {1, 2, 3, 4} for both tracks. Top-N
   co-occurrence is {3, 5, 10, 15} for ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8. For
   ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA it's {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30}: the original
   {3, 5, 10, 15} range was too narrow and was cutting off the actual
   best combination for that track.
4. **Comparison.** For each model and track we report the best-F1
   combination from the grid, and the per-CCS-category F1 at that
   combination.

**Correctness check.** The R port reproduces the published ClinicalBERT
numbers exactly (`scripts/run_sanity_check.R`: ICD-9->ICD-10-CA
P0.686/R0.277/F1 0.395/Acc 0.246; ICD-9->ICDA-8 P0.753/R0.680/F1
0.715/Acc 0.556, both at threshold 0.995). The grid results below were
also checked against independent Python reference numbers; see the
verification section.

## Results: best combination per model, per track

```{r best-table}
best_by_model %>%
  mutate(track = recode(track, `10_9` = "ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA", `8_9` = "ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8")) %>%
  select(Track = track, Model = model, `Similarity threshold` = similarity_threshold,
         `Top-N co-occurrence` = top_n, `Flag rule` = flag_combination,
         Precision = precision, Recall = recall, F1 = f1, Accuracy = accuracy) %>%
  arrange(Track, Model) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r fig-comparison, out.width="100%"}
include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS, "plot_f1_accuracy_comparison.png"))
```

SapBERT beats ClinicalBERT on both tracks at each model's best operating
point, with higher F1 and accuracy on both the ICD-10-CA and ICDA-8
target spaces. On ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA, both models score higher than
the numbers first reported here, since widening the top-N range on that
track turned up a better combination for both.

## Caveats

- **Not every category improves.** Some CCS categories score lower under
  SapBERT than ClinicalBERT. If you care about a specific category, check
  it on its own rather than relying on the overall numbers.
- **The "best combination" was picked using the same validation set it's
  scored on.** Threshold, top-N, and flag rule were all swept and the max
  F1 was chosen from that same manual crosswalk used to compute the
  metrics, so these numbers are optimistic. They aren't a held-out
  estimate of how well this would generalize to new codes. A more
  conservative comparison would fix one combination ahead of time instead
  of sweeping and picking the best.
- **A quirk in how the SapBERT embeddings were generated is worth
  knowing about.** Calling the PyTorch model directly through
  reticulate's R wrapper silently returns the wrong embeddings, with no
  error, just different numbers than calling the model normally in
  Python. The generation script avoids this by running the forward pass
  through a plain Python function instead (`py$fn(...)`), and the output
  was checked against a Python-native reference embedding to confirm it
  matches.
- **Co-occurrence, chapter filtering, and validation are identical
  between the two models.** Any difference in the results comes only
  from the embedding model used for the similarity signal.

## Verification against independent reference numbers

| Track | Model | Reference F1 / Acc | This report's F1 / Acc | Best combination |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ICD-9 -> ICD-10-CA | ClinicalBERT | 0.427 / 0.271 | 0.427 / 0.271 (match) | thr 0.995, top_n 30, flag 4 |
| ICD-9 -> ICD-10-CA | SapBERT | 0.530 / 0.360 | 0.530 / 0.360 (match) | thr 0.95, top_n 30, flag 4 |
| ICD-9 -> ICDA-8 | ClinicalBERT | 0.716 / 0.557 | 0.716 / 0.557 (match) | thr 0.999, top_n 5, flag 3 |
| ICD-9 -> ICDA-8 | SapBERT | 0.821 / 0.697 | 0.821 / 0.697 (match) | thr 0.99, top_n 3, flag 2 |

**All four reference numbers now reproduce exactly.** This resolves a
discrepancy that was previously flagged as an open question for the PI, so
it is worth recording what the problem actually was.

The reference ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA numbers were, for a while, not
reproducible: re-running the pipeline gave F1 0.423/0.268 (ClinicalBERT) and
0.523/0.355 (SapBERT) instead of 0.427/0.271 and 0.530/0.360. The cause was
**the parameter grid, not the numbers**. `scripts/02_run_comparison.R` swept
top-N {3, 5, 10, 15}, and on this track the true optimum for both models sits
at **top_n = 30**, outside that range. The narrow grid could not reach the
optimum, so the best it could report was a slightly worse combination. The
reference numbers were right all along; the search that was supposed to
confirm them was too small.

Two earlier attempts to check this were themselves unreliable, and both are
now superseded:

- The first "fix" edited the narrative and `results/best_by_model.csv` to
  describe a widened top-N range, but never changed the script, so no
  committed code produced the numbers being claimed.
- The second attempt did widen the script's range, but the re-run was
  interrupted partway (it completed only 1 of 4 thresholds for the first of
  four model/track combinations) and its partial output was mistakenly read
  as a finished result. That is where the conclusion "the wider range does
  not reproduce the claimed numbers" came from. **That conclusion was
  wrong** -- it was drawn from a run that never finished.

Both tracks now sweep top-N {3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30}, a strict superset of
every range used previously, so nothing reachable before can be lost. The
sweep completes for every model and track, and the numbers above come from
that completed sweep. They are additionally corroborated by an independent
script (`scripts/07_full_grid_comparison.R`, which scores every embedding
condition on the same grid) reaching identical values by a different code
path.

The wider grid was affordable only because of a performance fix: chapter
lookup in `merge_and_flag()` used to run one small `dplyr::filter()` per
candidate row under `rowwise()`, costing ~10-12s per grid point. It is now
vectorized (computed once per distinct code and recycled), which is ~130x
faster. That is a pure-speed change with no methodological content, and
`scripts/verify_vectorized_equivalence.R` gates it: it runs the old and new
implementations side by side on real data for both tracks and both
directions and asserts the chapter lookups, the full `merge_and_flag()`
output, and all four metrics under all four flag rules are identical. All
18 checks pass.

## Task 1 + 2: filler-word stripping and a general-purpose embedding model

```{r extended-setup, include=FALSE}
have_extended <- file.exists(file.path(RESULTS, "full_grid_best.csv"))
if (have_extended) {
  fg_best        <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "full_grid_best.csv"))
  fg_stripping   <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "full_grid_stripping.csv"))
  fg_paired      <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "full_grid_stripping_paired.csv"))
  fg_family      <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "full_grid_family.csv"))
  fg_sensitivity <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "full_grid_sensitivity.csv"))
  pretty_track <- function(x) recode(x, `10_9` = "ICD-9 -> ICD-10-CA", `8_9` = "ICD-9 -> ICDA-8")
}
```

Filler words (see `scripts/filler_words.json` -- "and", "or", "with",
"unspecified", "other", "nos", etc.) were stripped from ICD code label text
before embedding, and a third, non-medical embedding model
(`sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2`) was added as a comparison arm
alongside ClinicalBERT and SapBERT, to test whether domain-specific medical
pretraining actually helps on this short-text matching task.

**Every condition below was scored on the identical full grid** -- thresholds
{0.95, 0.99, 0.995, 0.999} x top-N {3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30} x all 4 flag
rules = 112 combinations per condition per track, 1,792 evaluations in total
(`scripts/07_full_grid_comparison.R`). An earlier version of this comparison
could only afford one fixed (threshold, top_n) point per track, which was a
real weakness: each model has a different similarity distribution, so the
operating point that suits one need not suit another, and a single-point
comparison can rank models by an artifact of that choice. The
operating-point sensitivity table below shows this was not a hypothetical
worry -- 6 of 16 model/track rankings change between the two approaches.

```{r extended-table, eval=have_extended}
fg_best %>%
  mutate(Track = pretty_track(track)) %>%
  select(Track, Model = model, Threshold = similarity_threshold, `Top-N` = top_n,
         Flag = flag_combination, Precision = precision, Recall = recall,
         F1 = f1, Accuracy = accuracy) %>%
  arrange(Track, desc(F1)) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Best combination per embedding condition, full grid")
```

```{r extended-missing, eval=!have_extended, results='asis'}
cat("_Not yet run -- see `scripts/07_full_grid_comparison.R` then",
    "`scripts/08_assemble_full_grid.R`. Needs `data/generated/*.xlsx`",
    "from `scripts/generate_embeddings.py` first._")
```

**How to read this table.** All eight conditions ran the identical grid, so
every comparison here is apples-to-apples. The conditions are:

- **ClinicalBERT-original** / **SapBERT-base** -- the two arms the existing
  baseline was built on. ClinicalBERT-original's matrices came from an
  external pipeline not present in this repo, whose generation method is
  undocumented (still flagged in `PI_QUESTIONS.md`); SapBERT-base's
  generation is documented and validated here.
- **ClinicalBERT-base**, **SapBERT-base-regen**, **mpnet-base** and their
  **-stripped** counterparts -- all regenerated with the same script and
  pooling (`scripts/generate_embeddings.py`), so base-vs-stripped isolates
  the filler-word effect and family-vs-family isolates the model effect,
  with no other differences.

**Two useful controls came out of running everything on one grid.**
`SapBERT-base-regen` lands *exactly* on `SapBERT-base` -- identical F1,
accuracy, best parameters and grid median on both tracks -- confirming the
regeneration pipeline reproduces the validated `data/sapbert` matrices
bit-for-bit, so the regenerated arms are trustworthy. `ClinicalBERT-base`
lands very close to but not exactly on `ClinicalBERT-original`
(F1 0.430 vs 0.427 on ICD-10-CA, 0.716 on both for ICDA-8); that small gap
is the original pipeline's undocumented generation choices, not an effect of
anything in this task, and should not be attributed to filler stripping.

### Findings

#### Filler-word stripping (task 1): helps ClinicalBERT, hurts SapBERT, model-dependent

```{r stripping-table, eval=have_extended}
fg_stripping %>%
  mutate(Track = pretty_track(track)) %>%
  select(Track, Family = family, `Best F1 (base)` = best_f1_base,
         `Best F1 (stripped)` = best_f1_stripped, `Delta best F1` = delta_best_f1,
         `Mean F1 (base)` = mean_f1_base, `Mean F1 (stripped)` = mean_f1_stripped,
         `Delta mean F1` = delta_mean_f1) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Filler-word stripping: best-point and whole-grid means")
```

Best-point comparisons alone are a weak read on an effect this small -- one
arm can win simply by finding a luckier corner of the grid. The stronger
test is **paired**: at each of the 112 matched (threshold, top-N, flag)
points, did stripping help or hurt?

```{r stripping-paired, eval=have_extended}
fg_paired %>%
  mutate(Track = pretty_track(track)) %>%
  select(Track, Family = family, `Points` = n_points,
         `Stripped better` = stripped_better, Tied = tied,
         `Base better` = base_better, `Mean delta F1` = mean_delta_f1) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Filler-word stripping, paired at matched grid points")
```

The paired view is decisive in a way the best-point view is not, and the
direction depends on the model:

- **ClinicalBERT: stripping consistently helps.** On ICD-10-CA it wins at
  **112 of 112** matched points (mean +0.017 F1) -- as close to a clean
  result as this grid can produce -- and on ICDA-8 at 86 of 112 (+0.005).
- **SapBERT: stripping consistently hurts on ICDA-8.** It loses at **111 of
  112** points (mean -0.012 F1). On ICD-10-CA it mildly helps (85 of 112,
  +0.007).
- **mpnet: stripping hurts on ICD-10-CA** (105 of 112 points worse) and is a
  genuine wash on ICDA-8 (27 better, 33 tied, 52 worse, mean -0.0006).

A plausible reading is that stripping helps exactly the model that needs the
help. ClinicalBERT is the weakest arm here, and removing low-content tokens
("and", "or", "with", "unspecified", "nos" -- see
`scripts/filler_words.json`) evidently sharpens its representations.
SapBERT was trained specifically to align biomedical entity names, so it
already handles those tokens; deleting them just removes information it was
using. That is a hypothesis suggested by the pattern, not something these
runs establish.

**Recommendation: do not adopt filler stripping globally.** It is not a
general improvement -- it is model-specific, and for the current
best-performing configuration (SapBERT on ICDA-8) it is actively harmful.
It is worth keeping as a per-model option. Note also that these are
aggregate numbers; an aggregate F1 shift this small can hide larger
per-CCS-category swings in both directions, which is worth checking before
any adoption decision.

#### General-purpose vs. domain-specific embeddings (task 2)

```{r family-table, eval=have_extended}
fg_family %>%
  mutate(Track = pretty_track(track)) %>%
  select(Track, Family = family, `Best condition` = model,
         Threshold = similarity_threshold, `Top-N` = top_n, Flag = flag_combination,
         Precision = precision, Recall = recall, F1 = f1, Accuracy = accuracy) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Best result per model family, full grid")
```

**The answer differs by track, and the anecdote holds up on one of them.**

- **ICD-9 -> ICD-10-CA: a statistical tie.** The general-purpose
  `mpnet-base` reaches F1 0.533 / Acc 0.363, against 0.534 for the best
  SapBERT arm and 0.530 for SapBERT-base. A 0.001-0.003 F1 gap on 937
  validation pairs is nothing -- these three are indistinguishable. A
  general-purpose sentence embedding model with no medical pretraining
  whatsoever matches the specialized biomedical model on this track.
- **ICD-9 -> ICDA-8: SapBERT wins clearly.** F1 0.821 vs. mpnet's 0.769, a
  0.052 gap that is far too large to be grid noise.
- **Both models beat ClinicalBERT everywhere**, by a wide margin (0.448 and
  0.722 at best). Whatever advantage ClinicalBERT's clinical-notes
  pretraining offers, it does not transfer to matching short ICD label
  strings.

So Dr. Lix's recollection that general-purpose models can beat specialized
medical ones at matching medical synonyms is **partly confirmed**: mpnet
fully matches SapBERT on ICD-10-CA and crushes ClinicalBERT on both tracks,
but it does not beat SapBERT, and on ICDA-8 it clearly loses. The honest
summary is that *domain-specific pretraining per se is not what matters* --
ClinicalBERT is domain-specific and is the worst arm by a distance. What
matters is what the model was trained to do: SapBERT was trained explicitly
to align biomedical **entity names**, which is precisely this task, and it
is the only arm that is never beaten. This connects to Zhang et al. (2019)'s
point (see Background) that this combination of co-occurrence and embedding
similarity remains an open question -- on one of the two tracks the
embedding source genuinely does not matter, and the surrounding architecture
(co-occurrence + chapter filtering + flag rules) is doing the work.

#### How much did the operating point matter?

```{r sensitivity-table, eval=have_extended}
fg_sensitivity %>%
  mutate(Track = pretty_track(track)) %>%
  select(Track, Model = model, `Best F1` = best_f1, `Median F1` = f1_median,
         `Min F1` = f1_min, `Max F1` = f1_max, `F1 at shared point` = shared_point_f1,
         `Rank (best)` = rank_by_best, `Rank (shared point)` = rank_at_shared,
         `Rank changed` = rank_changed) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Best-over-grid vs. single-shared-point ranking")
```

This table is why the full grid was worth running. Scoring every condition
at one shared operating point instead of searching per condition **changes
the ranking in 6 of 16 model/track rows**, and understates every condition's
F1 (by up to 0.014). The spread within a single condition is also large --
ClinicalBERT-stripped on ICD-10-CA ranges from F1 0.255 to 0.448 across the
grid, wider than the gap between any two model families. A single-point
comparison of these models would have been measuring the point as much as
the model.

**Remaining caveat, unchanged and important.** Every "best" number here is
chosen by sweeping parameters against the same validation set used to score
them, so all of these figures are optimistic and are not held-out estimates
of generalization. That applies equally to all eight conditions, so the
*comparisons* between them are fair; the *absolute* values are not
generalization estimates. Nothing in this task addressed that, and it
remains the single biggest methodological weakness in the pipeline.

## Task 3: bidirectional mapping and round-trip consistency

```{r roundtrip-setup, include=FALSE}
have_roundtrip <- file.exists(file.path(RESULTS, "bidirectional_roundtrip.csv"))
if (have_roundtrip) {
  roundtrip <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "bidirectional_roundtrip.csv"))
}
```

The reverse direction (ICD-10-CA -> ICD-9-CM, ICDA-8 -> ICD-9-CM) uses the
same rule-based pipeline as the forward direction -- chapter-distance
filtering, similarity threshold, top-N co-occurrence, flag rule -- just
normalized per target code instead of per ICD-9-CM code (see
`get_similarity_scores_from_sheets_reverse` etc. in `pipeline_lib.R`). It
reuses each track/model's already-chosen best forward parameters rather
than an independent reverse grid search, to keep runtime reasonable; this
means the reverse numbers below are not independently grid-optimized the
way the forward numbers are.

Round-trip consistency: for each ICD-9-CM code the forward pipeline maps to
some target code, does the reverse pipeline map that target code back to
the same ICD-9-CM code? This is a self-consistency signal independent of
the manual crosswalk.

```{r roundtrip-table, eval=have_roundtrip}
roundtrip %>%
  mutate(track = recode(track, `10_9` = "ICD-9-CM <-> ICD-10-CA", `8_9` = "ICD-9-CM <-> ICDA-8")) %>%
  select(Track = track, Model = model,
         `Fwd F1` = fwd_f1, `Fwd Acc` = fwd_accuracy,
         `Rev F1` = rev_f1, `Rev Acc` = rev_accuracy,
         `Round-trip rate` = roundtrip_rate,
         `Consistent / Total` = roundtrip_n_total) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r roundtrip-missing, eval=!have_roundtrip, results='asis'}
cat("_Not yet run -- see `scripts/05_bidirectional_and_roundtrip.R`._")
```

**Flagged for the PI, not guessed at.** Round-trip agreement is reported
here purely as a metric -- an extra column alongside F1/precision/recall/
accuracy -- and does **not** change which mappings the pipeline outputs. It
would also be possible to use round-trip agreement actively, e.g. only
accepting a forward mapping if the reverse pipeline agrees, which would
change the actual mapping output rather than just how it's scored. The task
didn't specify which is wanted, and the two have materially different
consequences (a metric is informational; a filter changes what downstream
users receive), so this report implements the metric-only version by
default. Please confirm with Dr. Lix whether round-trip agreement should
also be used as a filtering criterion before that version is built.
```

## Not implemented -- flagged for the PI

Two items from the task list are intentionally not implemented; see
`PI_QUESTIONS.md` for full detail:

- **Removing codes because "cosine similarity drops"** -- which codes, and
  the exact mechanism, weren't specified. Not guessed at, per instructions.
- **Expanded validation dataset** -- no additional verified crosswalk pairs
  beyond the existing 937 (ICD-9/10) and 331 (ICD-9/ICDA-8) were found
  anywhere in this repository. If Dr. Lix has more, point the pipeline at
  them and re-run; a drop in F1/accuracy as the validation set grows would
  be expected (an easier-subset effect), not a bug.
